frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control through Sonatrach, but European buyers seek alternative suppliers and greater upstream access. Hydrocarbon dependence continues to constrain long-term economic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Morocco pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger increases border-security costs, while the Morocco rivalry complicates regional infrastructure and diplomatic coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic corridor rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting US, European, and Chinese interest because of its access to critical-mineral supply chains. Infrastructure finance could improve connectivity while deepening external leverage over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Angola remains heavily dependent on declining oil output and foreign technical capital. Debt servicing, production-sharing agreements, and limited diversification reduce effective sovereign control over value creation.

frictionVectors.title: Niger trade and pipeline tensions
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain strained over cross-border trade and the operating environment around the Niger-Benin oil export route. The dispute exposes Benin’s vulnerability to regional political decisions beyond its control.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, logistics, and energy expansion relies substantially on foreign lenders, contractors, and trading partners. This supports growth but can narrow policy space during regional crises.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for a larger share of diamond value and greater domestic beneficiation as the traditional diamond market weakens. The negotiations test whether state leverage can translate into sustainable industrial gains.

frictionVectors.title: Resource diversification challenge
frictionVectors.details: Copper, coal, and other minerals offer diversification but require outside capital, infrastructure, and export access. Botswana’s stable institutions provide leverage, though its landlocked geography remains a structural constraint.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization pressure
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over industrial mining and gold revenues while confronting informal production and smuggling. Reduced transparency and security risks may deter responsible foreign investment without eliminating external extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian military support and private security networks is reshaping the country’s external alignment. The partnership may expand regime autonomy from Western actors but can create new financial, operational, and political dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi Security Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and border insecurity continue to constrain trade, coordination, and national security planning. The dispute increases Burundi's reliance on external diplomatic and security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-mineral activity remains vulnerable to informal extraction and opaque cross-border trading. Government efforts to formalize licensing are improving control but remain limited by weak enforcement capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Port and Digital Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: External investment in ports, logistics, telecommunications, and digital services strengthens connectivity but creates long-term leverage over critical infrastructure. Praia is seeking diversification to avoid overdependence on any single partner.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism-Linked Resource Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned tourism development supports growth while intensifying pressure on land, water, and coastal access. Rising dependence on imported energy and food limits the practical depth of economic sovereignty.

highlights: Oil and Timber Revenues Remain Externally Exposed

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Sector Dependence on Foreign Capital
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and emerging mining projects rely heavily on foreign firms, financing, and technical capacity. Contract opacity and weak oversight limit the state's ability to convert resource wealth into broad-based sovereign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Disrupted Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest and insurgency in the Far North threaten roads, pipelines, agricultural corridors, and border trade. Security spending and fragmented control reduce the government's effective command over strategic assets.

highlights: Minerals Remain Outside Formal State Control

frictionVectors.title: Russian Influence and Mining Access
frictionVectors.details: The government's security partnership with Russian personnel has strengthened regime protection while increasing concerns over preferential access to gold and diamonds. This arrangement narrows policy autonomy and weakens transparency around resource concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Transport Corridors Depend on External Security
frictionVectors.details: Roads linking Bangui to neighboring markets remain vulnerable to armed groups and require foreign-backed security support. Poor connectivity keeps producers dependent on intermediaries and limits national capture of commodity value.

highlights: Oil Revenue Anchors a Fragile Transition

frictionVectors.title: Oil Dependence and Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenue remains central to state finances, leaving Chad exposed to foreign operators, price volatility, and opaque production arrangements. Limited diversification weakens bargaining power over infrastructure and fiscal policy.

frictionVectors.title: French and Regional Security Rebalancing
frictionVectors.details: The drawdown and reconfiguration of French military ties has increased pressure on Chad to diversify security partnerships. Instability in Sudan and the Sahel raises the cost of protecting borders, trade routes, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte despite Comorian claims, shaping maritime access, migration policy, and regional security. The dispute continues to constrain Moroni's sovereignty narrative.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on foreign donors, Gulf partners, and external contractors for ports, energy, and transport infrastructure. Limited domestic capacity leaves strategic assets vulnerable to outside influence.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral sovereignty and Chinese-linked supply chains
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains central to foreign commercial influence, while Kinshasa seeks more revenue, processing, and contract leverage. Regulatory disputes and opaque beneficial ownership continue to limit sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: M23 conflict and regional intervention
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict in the east continues to threaten mining corridors, displacement patterns, and state authority. Rwanda-linked accusations, regional diplomacy, and competing external security interests complicate Kinshasa's efforts to secure territory.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: State revenue and export capacity remain heavily tied to offshore oil, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price shifts and foreign operator leverage. Limited diversification weakens long-term control over national resource development.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for roads, public works, and extractive logistics. Debt obligations and project opacity can narrow the government's room to renegotiate strategic infrastructure terms.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of export chains
frictionVectors.details: Cocoa, oil, mining, and port operations still depend substantially on multinational capital and external markets. Abidjan is expanding processing and value capture, but domestic firms remain comparatively weak.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover pressure
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability from Burkina Faso and Mali are increasing pressure on northern borders and transport corridors. Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening security partnerships while guarding against excessive external dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and port concentration
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through foreign military bases and port concessions, but this creates dependence on external powers and exposes the country to regional rivalries. Competition among China, the United States, France, and Gulf actors is intensifying.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopian corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Most commercial activity remains tied to Ethiopia's trade through Djibouti's ports and logistics network. This provides essential revenue but leaves sovereignty and fiscal stability vulnerable to Ethiopian political shifts and alternative corridor development.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian operation of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, viewing upstream control as a strategic threat to national water security. Negotiations remain vulnerable to regional tensions and changing Sudanese alignments.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and strategic-asset exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs increase reliance on Gulf capital, multilateral lenders, and asset monetization. This strengthens short-term liquidity but can dilute independent control over infrastructure and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature fields and limited diversification are reducing state revenue while foreign operators retain technical and capital advantages. The government is seeking new offshore investment but remains exposed to volatile production and prices.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and public works remain central to the country's development model. Their strategic value gives Beijing durable commercial and diplomatic influence despite Malabo's formal control.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping routes draw interest from Gulf, Egyptian, and other regional actors. External security competition raises Asmara's leverage but also increases pressure over port access and alignments.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque mining partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide vital foreign exchange but operate amid persistent scrutiny over labor practices, state involvement, and revenue transparency. Reliance on a narrow group of foreign partners limits bargaining flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: South African economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade corridors, customs revenue, finance, and energy links remain heavily tied to South Africa and the wider SACU system. Pretoria's economic weight limits Mbabane's room for independent industrial and foreign-policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: Political legitimacy pressure
frictionVectors.details: Restrictions on political competition and labor activism continue to create friction with international partners and civil-society networks. Domestic instability could affect investor confidence in strategic sectors and transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The dam expands Ethiopia's control over electricity generation and strengthens its upstream bargaining position. Egypt and Sudan remain concerned about operating rules, drought management, and the absence of a binding long-term agreement.

frictionVectors.title: Port-access and regional rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for reliable Red Sea access continues to strain relations with Somalia and complicate ties with Eritrea, Egypt, and Gulf actors. Commercial corridors and port concessions are increasingly tied to sovereignty and security calculations.

frictionVectors.title: Mining contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater domestic value capture from manganese, iron ore, and hydrocarbons. Renegotiation risks investor delays and tension with established French, Chinese, and other foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export capacity remains tied to foreign-financed rail, port, and logistics networks. Disruptions or unfavorable concession terms could limit Libreville's control over strategic commodity flows.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fleets and opaque licensing arrangements continue to threaten coastal fisheries, a critical food and livelihood resource. Weak monitoring capacity limits effective Gambian control over its maritime zone.

frictionVectors.title: Port and border dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country's trade routes and security environment remain heavily shaped by Senegal, while foreign aid and investment support key infrastructure. This dependence constrains independent bargaining over transport and development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Gold value-chain leakage
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining and informal exports undermine environmental governance, tax collection, and state control of Ghana's largest mineral resource. Foreign trading networks and equipment suppliers complicate enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Prospective lithium and other mineral projects are attracting external capital before domestic processing capacity is established. Accra faces pressure to balance investment needs with stronger local-content and beneficiation requirements.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mineral corridors
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite and iron-ore expansion depends on foreign consortia, railways, ports, and long-term offtake agreements. The state is gaining revenue and infrastructure but remains exposed to external control of export logistics and pricing.

frictionVectors.title: Military rule and investor risk
frictionVectors.details: The junta's political transition and centralized contract-making create uncertainty over institutional oversight. Social tensions around land, compensation, and mining employment could intensify as Simandou-related construction accelerates.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew export dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly dependent on raw cashew exports, leaving producers vulnerable to foreign buyers, volatile prices, and limited domestic processing. This weakens sovereign leverage over the country's principal export.

frictionVectors.title: Port and political fragility
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's port infrastructure and customs system are vulnerable to political interference and external commercial pressure. Governance instability also sustains concerns about trafficking networks and foreign influence over strategic logistics.

highlights: Port and energy assets remain strategic

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure and reliance on multilateral lenders constrain fiscal sovereignty. Major transport, energy, and digital infrastructure projects remain exposed to foreign financing and procurement influence.

frictionVectors.title: Resource and land concession tensions
frictionVectors.details: Mining, geothermal, carbon-market, and large-scale agricultural projects face scrutiny over community consent, revenue sharing, and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but deepen dependence on South African infrastructure, financing, and market access. Delays, cost overruns, and local displacement continue to drive sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and fiscal vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic generation and a narrow economic base leave Lesotho vulnerable to external contractors and imported power. Fiscal dependence reduces negotiating room over infrastructure and resource agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led iron ore, gold, and mineral projects promise export revenue but raise persistent concerns over contract transparency, local benefits, and environmental enforcement. Weak administrative capacity limits effective state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia-area port development and corridor projects attract competing foreign commercial interests. Liberia risks trading long-term control of strategic logistics assets for short-term investment and budget support.

highlights: External patrons shape security and exports

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks can disrupt fields, pipelines, terminals, and export decisions. The national oil sector remains the principal source of state revenue but also the central bargaining tool among factions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and commercial influence
frictionVectors.details: External security partners and regional sponsors continue to influence territorial control and political negotiations. Energy access, reconstruction contracts, and migration cooperation are frequently linked to these relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and revenue capture
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects provide export earnings but expose Madagascar to foreign corporate leverage and volatile commodity markets. Communities continue to contest compensation, land access, and the distribution of royalties.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal logging and frontier extraction
frictionVectors.details: Rosewood trafficking, illicit gold mining, and pressure on protected forests undermine state authority and conservation commitments. Weak enforcement allows transnational brokers and local political networks to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms are positioning around uranium, rare earths and graphite as Malawi seeks to formalize licensing and increase domestic value capture. Limited regulatory capacity and financing needs leave the state vulnerable to unequal contracts.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and Power Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Fuel shortages, hydropower vulnerability and reliance on imported inputs constrain national resilience. IMF-led reforms and donor support improve macroeconomic discipline but reduce policy room.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is pressing foreign mining companies for larger state participation and revenue shares, raising tensions over permits, taxes and operating conditions. Production remains strategically vital but is exposed to insecurity and contract uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Mali's reliance on Russian security support has reduced Western leverage but deepened dependence on an external military partner. Persistent insurgency threatens transport corridors, mining zones and state control beyond major cities.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers fiscal and energy leverage, but cross-border revenue management and operator dependence limit immediate sovereignty gains. Local-content expectations may generate political pressure as exports scale.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Corridor Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and planned green-hydrogen infrastructure require major foreign capital, ports and transmission links. These projects can diversify the economy while leaving Mauritania exposed to external demand, financing terms and security risks along transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime-Sovereignty Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos settlement process and the future of Diego Garcia remain central to Mauritius's sovereignty and strategic bargaining position. Security arrangements must balance national claims with continued foreign military use.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Financial Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius depends on international shipping, offshore finance and imported energy, making it sensitive to disruptions in Indian Ocean routes and external regulatory pressure. Its diversified institutions and maritime capabilities provide substantial mitigation.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Politics
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is consolidating control over phosphate, fisheries, ports and renewable projects in Western Sahara while seeking wider international recognition of its position. The dispute continues to generate legal, diplomatic and regional friction.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital, Domestic Control
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf and Chinese investment is accelerating ports, energy and industrial infrastructure, but creates competition over strategic assets and export corridors. Rabat retains strong state direction while managing dependence on external technology and finance.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Gas Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten LNG infrastructure and transport routes, increasing reliance on foreign security partners. The state is seeking to preserve national control while managing major external energy investors.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Revenue Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Expectations for local jobs, state revenue, and community benefits remain high around LNG and mining projects. Weak oversight and opaque contracting risk reinforcing perceptions of external extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Offshore discoveries are attracting major foreign capital, creating pressure for stronger local-content rules and a larger state share. Windfalls remain prospective, while environmental and fiscal risks are becoming more politically salient.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects depend on foreign finance, technology, and export infrastructure. Namibia is asserting policy control, but project execution could leave substantial value captured offshore.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta is renegotiating or challenging established foreign mining relationships while seeking greater national control over uranium and other resources. Political uncertainty and sanctions complicate investment, revenue collection, and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Attacks by jihadist groups threaten roads, energy infrastructure, and border trade. Reduced Western security cooperation and reliance on alternative external partners have increased operational risk.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Production remains vulnerable to theft, sabotage, and aging infrastructure, limiting the state's ability to capture full resource value. International oil companies, traders, and contractors retain significant leverage over capital and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for rail, power, and transport projects. These partnerships expand infrastructure capacity but can create debt, procurement, and strategic-dependence concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Mineral Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: International pressure over alleged links between eastern Congo armed networks and regional mineral flows continues to challenge Rwanda's diplomatic and commercial position. Traceability demands could affect mineral exports and foreign investment.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda maintains strong administrative control over infrastructure and development planning but remains reliant on aid, concessional finance, and foreign investment. Shifts in donor policy could narrow fiscal and strategic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: External Offshore Licensing
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest in São Tomé and Príncipe’s offshore blocks offers potential revenue but leaves the state dependent on foreign capital, technology, and contractual expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported fuel and externally financed infrastructure limits economic autonomy, while Gulf of Guinea maritime-security partnerships bring competing outside interests.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Cross-Border Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Mauritania is strategically important but exposes Dakar to disputes over revenue allocation, operating control, and foreign-operator terms.

frictionVectors.title: Contract Renegotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government’s sovereignty-focused review of mining and petroleum agreements may strengthen state control but risks friction with international investors and financing partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Tuna Access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles gains substantial revenue from foreign fishing fleets, but limited enforcement capacity creates persistent concerns over stock depletion, licensing terms, and unequal value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Indian, French, Chinese, and other maritime-security interests enhance surveillance and infrastructure options while increasing pressure on Mahé to preserve strategic neutrality.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects remain central to growth, but foreign capital and concession structures can leave Sierra Leone exposed to revenue leakage and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining-linked rail, port, and logistics investments improve export capacity while tying national infrastructure priorities to external operators and commodity cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Offshore petroleum licensing and Turkey’s expanding energy-security role could unlock resources, but weak institutions and federal disputes make ownership, revenue sharing, and environmental oversight contentious.

frictionVectors.title: Somaliland Maritime Contest
frictionVectors.details: Disputes involving Ethiopia, Somaliland, and Mogadishu over port access and maritime sovereignty draw in regional and Gulf powers, complicating Somalia’s control of its coastline and offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is balancing Western, Chinese, and domestic interests in platinum-group metals, manganese, and battery minerals while seeking greater local processing. Foreign investment remains necessary, limiting Pretoria's room for unilateral control.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, port congestion, and failing freight rail constrain mining sovereignty and export earnings. State-led reforms and private participation are improving capacity unevenly.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on Sudanese pipelines and export terminals, leaving its main revenue stream exposed to Sudan's war and external commercial leverage. Production disruptions and opaque contracting further weaken national control.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Uganda, Sudan, Kenya, and Gulf-linked commercial actors retain influence through security, trade, and oil relationships. Weak institutions and delayed political reforms make resource governance vulnerable to elite capture.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Smuggling Networks
frictionVectors.details: Gold revenues are financing rival armed actors and moving through regional and Gulf-linked trading channels outside effective civilian oversight. This externalizes Sudan's mineral wealth while sustaining the conflict economy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Pipeline Contest
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, oil infrastructure, and humanitarian corridors carries major strategic value for regional and international powers. Fighting and foreign-backed logistics are eroding any coherent sovereign management of national infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Development Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing international energy companies for stronger domestic benefits, local content, and revenue terms in its delayed offshore LNG project. Prolonged negotiations and regulatory uncertainty risk slowing development while preserving bargaining space.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Influence
frictionVectors.details: The expansion of Dar es Salaam-linked rail and port corridors is attracting competing Gulf, Chinese, and Western interests. Tanzania retains substantial control, but financing and construction dependencies could shape long-term access terms.

frictionVectors.title: Port-Centered External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo's regional leverage but depends heavily on foreign capital, shipping networks, and neighboring-country transit demand. Revenue gains have not fully translated into broader sovereign control over logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate Governance
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate remains strategically important, yet production and processing constraints limit domestic value capture. Foreign finance, technical partnerships, and opaque state-linked arrangements continue to shape the sector.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial and political support remains closely tied to migration control, limiting Tunisia's room for independent bargaining. A stalled or constrained IMF relationship further narrows fiscal options.

frictionVectors.title: Imported energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported hydrocarbons and electricity exposes Tunisia to external price shocks and supplier leverage. Domestic phosphate and renewable-energy potential remains undercapitalized.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and transit risk
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to national revenue ambitions but faces environmental opposition, financing constraints, and exposure to external contractors and lenders. Export dependence through Tanzania limits Uganda's strategic flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects expand Uganda's infrastructure base while increasing repayment and procurement dependence. Regional military commitments also divert resources from domestic development.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Renewed investment from Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked firms is expanding copper capacity, but Zambia still captures limited value beyond mining and concentrates. Efforts to increase local processing face power, capital, and infrastructure constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and electricity vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has improved external credibility but limits fiscal independence and policy flexibility. Hydropower shortages and regional transmission bottlenecks threaten mining output and industrial sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors dominate major lithium, platinum, and gold projects, giving Zimbabwe access to capital but leaving ownership, processing, and revenue capture heavily contested. Export restrictions have not yet produced a broad domestic refining base.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: U.S. and other Western sanctions, combined with arrears and weak market access, push Harare toward narrower external partnerships. Persistent currency instability increases dependence on foreign mining finance and informal resource channels.
